items.title: ‘Craving the Truth’: The Shocking Spiritual Hunger Sweeping Gen Z
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Naomi Anderson is on a mission to point Generation Z toward the truth.

Anderson is co-founder of Verity Collective, “a movement rooted in the unchanging truth of the Gospel.” She told CBN News she wants to bring Jesus to America’s young generation.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

“We believe that there is a lot of confusion and noise in this world for them, and we want to bring them back to the one and only truth, which is Jesus,” she said.

Anderson believes young people are “craving the truth” but have faced an uphill battle in understanding it, as they’ve been sold an improper understanding of reality.

“They are craving the truth. They just don’t know what it is because they’ve been told to define it for themselves,” she said. “So when we ask them, ‘What is truth?’ they literally will sit there on camera and it will take them minutes to try to decide right because they have been told truth is objective — you can define your own truth. … They just need to be pointed back to the truth.”

The need for truth couldn’t be more pressing, as many young people are suffering from mental health issues, including anxiety and depression.

“It all forms around this idea of what is my identity, and where am I grounded in, and they just don’t have a landing solid spot,” Anderson said.

She also noted that young men appear to be increasingly interested in the Christian faith.

“These men are craving solid biblical truth, and that only comes from reading your Bible, and picking up the word, and being taught it by a Bible teacher,” Anderson said.

Through Verity Collective, she’s hoping to visit college campuses across the US in September and have a presence to spark conversations.

“What we’re recognizing is that when you actually pull someone aside and start asking them questions like, ‘What is truth?’ they have a yearning to know what it is that you want them to know,” Anderson said. “They’ll ask … ‘What do you believe truth is?’ And it really does open up an opportunity for us to speak the Gospel of Jesus Christ to them. And they are excited to hear it.”

Find out more about Verity Collective here.

items.title: Christian Activist Sues Minnesota City for Putting ‘Price Tag’ on His Constitutional Rights
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: A Christian man from Minnesota was ordered to pay for his free speech rights — and now he's suing.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

A Christian man from Minnesota was ordered to pay for his free speech rights — and now he’s suing.

In a lawsuit filed by the Center for American Liberty, Bryan Conwell is accusing officials in Benson of severe First Amendment violations by placing a “price tag” on free speech after Cherie Stielow, now a city council member, forced him to purchase a commercial vendor’s license to practice his constitutionally protected right to free speech at the city’s farmers market, which Stielow facilitates.

“Government officials cannot force Americans to buy a license before they peacefully express their beliefs on public property,” Mark Trammell of the Center for American Liberty said in a statement about the case. “If they can silence Bryan today, they can silence anyone tomorrow.”

According to the legal complaint, Conwell regularly holds pro-life and Gospel-centered placards on public property and waits peacefully and silently, speaking only to those who initiate conversation with him. The suit states the Christian activist “blocks no one, threatens no one, and sells nothing,” adding, “He asks only to be left alone to speak.”

Conwell, according to court documents, initially paid the $20 fee in order to hold his signs on public property during the hours the market was operating. In 2023, when he filled out the form and complied with the financial request, Conwell “was unaware of what his rights were and was simply trying to ensure that he could convey his message,” the complaint states.

The city then allowed Conwell to be present at the market in September and October 2023, but only so long as he remained inside a vendor tent.

At the same time as the dustup with Stielow was underway, another thread of Conwell’s story was unraveling.

In late July 2023, when all this began, the street preacher stood in a grassy area near the farmers market and spoke using a sound amplifier. At about 30 minutes to an hour into his speaking, Police Chief Ian Hodge purportedly told him he was breaking the city’s 50-foot sound ordinance and needed a permit to continue, so Conwell stopped.

Then between Aug. 9 and Oct. 24 of that year, Conwell made four separate trips to city hall, where he repeatedly attempted to apply for and obtain said noise permit. According to court documents, he was seemingly given the runaround by the city clerk, who said she was not aware of any such permit. He was also told the relevant person was unavailable and on more than one occasion was asked for his contact information but received no follow-up communication.

That saga came to an abrupt end on Oct. 24, 2023, when Hodge and the city attorney informed Conwell no such permit existed.

When Conwell returned to Benson on July 9 of this year and was approached yet again by Stielow, who handed him a vendor permit and demanded $20, he declined outright, reminding her — as in 2023 — he was not selling anything and would not be paying to hold a sign and speak peacefully with people on public property. He attempted the same thing on July 16.

Conwell received a trespass citation in both 2026 instances. He now faces up to 90 days in jail and up to $2,000 in fines.

Even one of the officers who cited Conwell purportedly expressed confusion to the preacher over the city’s policy against speech that should be protected by the Constitution.

“To be honest, man, I want clarification, too,” the officer told Conwell, according to court filings. “There are crimes of trespassing and crimes of disorderly conduct, but also you have your First Amendment right, so we’ve got to try to figure that out. … I know what you’re doing, I get it. I’m glad someone is out here doing it.”

items.title: The Company We Keep
items.author: Marvin Williams
items.summary: A scientific study revealed that watching TV programs featuring mean characters can actually lead people to be mean. Various forms of aggression—whether outright fighting or subtle gossip—primes viewers’ brains for similar behavior. This connection is often subconscious, meaning th
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

A scientific study revealed that watching TV programs featuring mean characters can actually lead people to be mean. Various forms of aggression—whether outright fighting or subtle gossip—primes viewers’ brains for similar behavior. This connection is often subconscious, meaning that even shows with seemingly “harmless” jokes at others’ expense can subtly influence how we treat others. So too, the people we choose to spend our time with will affect our behavior.

Solomon provides timeless wisdom on this important subject: “Walk with the wise and become wise, for a companion of fools suffers harm” (Proverbs 13:20). He implies that individuals may not achieve this wisdom alone, so they should associate with wise, God-honoring people—teachers and friends—instead of those who are foolish. Surrounding oneself with wise individuals fosters “good judgment” and helps us steer clear of “destruction” (v. 15). One scholar calls this “education by friendship.” Regular companions inevitably influence each other, for better or worse. Solomon urges us to be aware of the company we keep, recognizing that “the teaching of the wise is a fountain of life” (v. 14).  

As God helps us, let’s consistently surround ourselves with people who will encourage us to revere Him, love others, and grow in wisdom.

items.title: Recovering from Betrayal
items.author: Sheridan Voysey
items.summary: In one of her novels, Toni Morrison tells the story of Nel and Sula, girlfriends since childhood. But the friendship frays as Sula’s self-centeredness grows, culminating in her seducing Nel’s husband. “Why didn’t you think about me?” Nel asks Sula. “Didn’t I
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

In one of her novels, Toni Morrison tells the story of Nel and Sula, girlfriends since childhood. But the friendship frays as Sula’s self-centeredness grows, culminating in her seducing Nel’s husband. “Why didn’t you think about me?” Nel asks Sula. “Didn’t I count?” Sadly, Sula doesn’t even care enough to answer.

As anyone who’s experienced it knows, the pain of a friend’s betrayal is hard to rival. King David felt such “malice and abuse” when a political conspiracy of “threats and lies” engulfed him (Psalm 55:10-11). The worst part was who was behind it. “If an enemy were insulting me, I could endure it,” he says. “But it is you, a man like myself, my companion, my close friend” (vv. 12-13).

How should we respond to such betrayal? While David takes his turmoil to God (vv. 16, 20), he prays retribution will fall on his betraying friend (v. 15). We see a different approach taken by Jesus. Faced with Judas’ betrayal, he says, “Do what you came for, friend,” refusing to retaliate in kind (Matthew 26:49-50).

Can a friendship recover from betrayal? Only if the offended can stay open to reconciliation and the offender proves their repentance over time. Sula’s lack of remorse means Nel must walk away. May God empower us to treasure our friendships and swiftly make amends for any hurt we cause.

items.title: You Really Don’t Need to Have an Opinion On Everything
items.author: Jonathan Malm
items.summary: I play a game with a few of my friends. It’s not a game they enjoy, but I love it. I’ll frequently bring up current events that haven’t actually happened. For instance, I’ll ask, “Have you heard that Trump is trying to lower the age for smoking?” Some of my friends erupt into anger, while…
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

I play a game with a few of my friends. It’s not a game they enjoy, but I love it. I’ll frequently bring up current events that haven’t actually happened. For instance, I’ll ask, “Have you heard that Trump is trying to lower the age for smoking?”

Some of my friends erupt into anger, while the others rush to defend. I’ll usually argue back and forth with them for a few minutes before informing them that it was all a lie. Fake news.

Again, it’s a game I love, but none of my friends are too into it. I’m frankly surprised I still have friends because of this.

I play this game to show my overly opinionated friends that there’s very rarely rationality attached to their opinions. My hope is they would start to see that they’re quick to form opinions and maybe they shouldn’t be. Unfortunately, never once has that happened. I’ve never had a friend become less opinionated because of my harassment. 

You might be asking, what’s wrong with being overly opinionated? Opinions don’t really hurt anything.

I actually believe opinions can be toxic, especially from believers. Christians don’t really have the luxury of a public opinion. We are called to be ambassadors for Christ. We’re His representatives, which means we represent His truth. Not our own. As soon as you let your opinions rule a conversation, you’re speaking for yourself and not for God.

You can’t briefly shed your status as a Christ-ambassador to share your opinion. As a believer, you are perceived as a representative 100 percent of the time.

That means when you comment on that online article, those who know you’re a believer believe you’re speaking for Christ. Are you sure your opinions line up with the way Jesus thinks and feels about that situation?

There are some things that are clear in the Bible. But there are a whole lot more that the Bible doesn’t address. It’s nearly impossible to avoid having opinions on extra-biblical topics. But we don’t the luxury of fighting for those opinions. If we’re representatives of Christ, we don’t get to.

What about those issues that appear black and white? Do we at least get to air our viewpoints about those things?

I want to challenge you with this idea: Christians don’t have to bathe the world in black and white. God paints with a canvas of infinitely glorious colors—more colors than our eyes can perceive. Shouldn’t we paint with those same colors?

My job as a believer is not to project black and white onto others. It’s not even my job to convict the world of sin. That’s the Holy Spirit’s job. As it says in Matthew 5:13-16, my job is simply to be salt and light. I’m supposed to bring out the God-flavors and God-colors in this world. Salt doesn’t create flavor. It opens the taste buds to receive it. Light doesn’t create color. It simply reveals it.

You don’t have to vigilantly point out black and white to the world. If you’re functioning in your role as a light, your presence will expose it. Truth is truth, and it defends itself.

When we approach everything as black and white, we miss out on seeing the colors God created. Morality has never led anyone to Christ, but Christ leads people to morality. Our job is not to point out morality to the world. We are meant to show people Christ’s love. Bring them to the Savior. Then He’ll take them the rest of the way.

To be honest, I’m still wrestling with this idea. It’s a difficult thing to do because for so long I thought my job was to point out good and evil to people. Black and white. But being light that brings out God’s colors requires creativity in my conversations with people.

It’s tempting for any believer to quote Scripture or point out black and white in those situations. “The Bible says …” or “You’re still responsible for your own soul …” But that’s never what they need. They need to see the love of Christ in my life in the form of a listening, compassionate ear. My opinions and rationality rarely fixes emotional situations. In those instances, compassion and acceptance are the cure.

My Christian apologetics become literal apologies for the way fellow Christians have treated them. Once I’ve established common ground and they invite my input into their lives, I can mention that Jesus didn’t tell us to treat people that way. Somewhere in the middle of deftly navigating those conversations, their hearts become open. They start seeing the God-colors in the world through my words. 

Sometimes the conversations even turn to their real-life problems. They’ll open up about obstacles they face in their relationships or career. That’s when I have the opportunity to show them hidden options. I connect God’s creative power inside of me to their problems and expose the God-colors in the situation.

God can do the same through you if you make yourself available. Choose to point out the God-colors instead of the black and white. Bring out the flavors in the world. Be the most creative you can be in displaying Christ to a hurt and hopeless world.

items.title: Three Key Ways Nolan’s ‘Odyssey’ Is Timelessly Compelling
items.author: Dr. Kody W. Cooper
items.summary:
Dr. Kody W. Cooper

The film is true to the original in three key ways in which it portrays the world and captures the imagination: as moralistic, as providentially governed, and familistic.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Kody W. Cooper

Before the new The Odyssey even debuted and the IMAX theaters flickered to life, like the rose-fingered dawn, the critics were circling like hungry gulls who spot a shimmery sheen in the water and dive for a meal but startle when it is not a school of fish but tiger sharks awaiting them, and then they try to escape but cannot and are devoured. Just so, Nolan’s ambitious retelling of the Homeric epic didn’t flop as some predicted, with audiences either not caring about or overlooking the woke casting, and the naysayers were confounded and wrecked. But why has Nolan’s Odyssey broadly resonated with audiences and critics alike?

In my estimation, it is because Nolan’s Odyssey stays true to most of the essentials of the original epic, which enduringly resonates with audiences in how it compellingly speaks to the unchanging human condition. While there are certain liberties taken, Nolan’s Odyssey is true to the original in three key ways in which it portrays the world of Odysseus and captures the imagination: as moralistic, as providentially governed, and familistic. 

The moral axiom of the film is Zeus’s law, which is a rule of hospitality with a formulation similar to the Golden Rule. In the original work, Zeus’s law, or Xenia, was explicitly invoked by Odysseus when he and his men stumbled upon the Cyclops’s lair: “for Zeus is the avenger of all supplicants and foreigners in distress” (Fagles translation). The idea was that it was practically reasonable to treat strangers with kindness and respect because one ought to treat others as you would want to be treated. As the wheel of fortuna turns, one never knows when one will be sick, impoverished, a supplicant at the mercy of others. And particularly in the Bronze Age world, where travel entailed meeting strangers in strange lands, without an overarching authority to enforce the moral law, the moral norms of hospitality and reciprocity were essential to basic order.

In the film, Odysseus intends to invoke Zeus’s law, but the Cyclops offers no dialogue and simply sets about eating them. But in the original, the Cyclops articulates his rejection of Zeus’s law: “We Cyclopes do not care about Jove or any of your blessed gods, for we are ever so much stronger than they.” Odysseus perceives (correctly) that the beast has monstrously flouted the moral law and blinds him out of self-defense. Still, in his triumph escaping the beast, Odysseus cannot resist a taunt that goads the Cyclops into a rage that unnecessarily endangers his men. The great man reputed to be the most cunning among men is not immune to hubristic folly.

So the moral law is connected to the gods’ apparent concern for and enforcement of it. In the original and the film, this is manifest on the occasion when their ship is grounded on Thrinacia. On the island is a sacred flock of cattle who belong to Helios, the sun god, and Odysseus is warned by a prophet not to eat the cattle. His men promise not to and resist for a time until their provisions run out, then they sneak to eat the cattle while Odysseus sleeps. “Did you think if you ate quietly, the sun god wouldn’t notice?” Odysseus wryly asks. The film does not relate the dialogues among the gods—but Helios complains to Zeus of the injustice, and he punishes the crew by sending a storm to wreck their ship. The island offered them refuge but they had transgressed the limits placed by the god. This violated Zeus’s law, and Zeus executed judgment by sinking their ship. Odysseus washes up on Calypso’s shores. 

So the Bronze Age world of the Mediterranean didn’t lack for an overarching enforcing principle of the moral law. It was providentially governed by the gods or god (Zeus). This doesn’t mean that the gods were necessarily righteous, however, as is apparent through Homer’s epics. In the Iliad, for example, gods like Hera stoke the conflict between the Greeks and Trojans and sabotage peaceful resolution of the conflict out of petty grievance and anger. In The Odyssey, rather than acknowledge that Odysseus justly blinded his son the Cyclops, Poseidon executes petty vengeance upon Odysseus, thwarting his return home for years. And the goddess Calypso effectively turns Odysseus into her sex slave for seven years, echoing the common theme of gods seducing and raping humans.

Assuming, as we can, that there are strong reasons to reject polytheism, what is the underlying reality behind the supernatural forces in Homeric myth? Perhaps, as St. Justin Martyr suggested, the Homeric epics were a pagan echo of the biblical truth that some angels fell, somehow begot children with women, enticed them to worship them, and established dominion over the human race. The various gods then are so many demons, albeit, demons subject to a superintending divine power. Or perhaps, as the Stoics and St. Clement of Alexandria contended, the various gods and goddesses were not literal divine beings but symbolic expressions of various aspects of the universal, governing divine logos. In this vein, perhaps Homer poetically veiled the deeper divine mysteries, which would be rash to divulge to the vulgar. So Neoplatonists like Proclus would contend that the various strife between the Olympian gods symbolized the order of providence, e.g., the conflict between Athena and Ares represents the distinction between God’s governance through intellectual causes and through necessary material causes. Or, when Athena appears in mortal forms to guide Odysseus, some Neoplatonists suggested this was actually a daemon, a sort of intermediary angelic entity carrying out the divine will, similar to a guardian angel.

Regardless of which of these is closest to the truth, the Ithacan’s world is clearly providentially governed. For his part, Nolan seems to adopt something like the guardian angel interpretation of Athena. In the original, Athena is portrayed as a pretty active co-belligerent with Odysseus, deflecting enemy spears, co-plotting his revenge, and orchestrating events under the sovereignty of Zeus. But Nolan’s Athena (played by Zendaya) appears as more of a moral guide to Odysseus, who takes on the form of a young woman who was killed during the sack of Troy. 

The film opens with the bard singing: “A face, a fleet, a war, a man, a thought, a trick—a trick to break the walls of Troy and burn it screaming to the ground!” Athena acts to convict Odysseus’s conscience that his trick, the cunning deceit of the Trojans to accept a sacred religious offering, was a violation of Zeus’s law that would unleash the marauding furies that come with widespread flouting of the Golden Rule, the destruction wrought by the Seafaring Peoples. Providential governance is deeply intertwined with moral illumination.

And when Odysseus questions the ways of the gods and the inability of man to understand their communication, Athena replies: “Who doesn’t understand thunder? Or fire? A child’s smile? A good harvest?” In other words, the providence and benevolence of God is manifest not only through conscience, but also through secondary causes and the blessings of the created order.

The world of the Achaeans is, finally, familistic. Hearth and home are the center of human flourishing and therefore threats or harms to its proper functioning drive much of the conflict, sorrow, tragedy, and heroism of human life. (This is actually a theme that runs through much of Nolan’s oeuvre, particularly in his best movies. In the Batman trilogy, Bruce Wayne’s fight as Batman is at root in defense of the human home and family against the violent crime that robbed him of his; and the relationship that sustains him is actually his sonhood to his adoptive father, Alfred. In Interstellar, the central moral conflict is that Cooper is called upon to sacrifice his relationship with his daughter to save her and the world. And in Inception, Cobb can only return to his home and children if he lets go of the haunting dream memory of his dead wife.)

In Nolan’s Odyssey, dysfunction and chaos reign in the home of the absent father and king. But the love and devotion of his son Telemachus and wife Penelope transcend the trappings and deceptions of the nymphean goddess Calypso. The allurements of pleasure, distraction, and sin are placed in the path of every husband and father and must be overcome if he is to perform his most basic duty: to protect and govern his home. 

Like when the copper-tendrilled dusk first appears, and then the horizon transforms into deep crimson before darkness falls. Or when the flaxen lion stalks the gazelles unseen, contentedly and casually fattening themselves on the amber grains of the field, which are then showered in pools of garnet when the lion pounces. So golden-haired and pinned Odysseus descends upon the wicked suitors and delivers a just and bloody end to their bacchanal. As Homer’s epic fades to black, the clear message is that the hero is the person who risks whatever it takes to save and protect his wife and children. We are reminded of the bard’s words: “A man.”

items.title: Nolan’s ‘Odyssey’: Seeing Homer’s Story Through Epic Tradition
items.author: Dr. Alex Taylor
items.summary:
Dr. Alex Taylor

Nolan's portrayal of the good of hospitality, the danger of rational control’s abuse of that good, and the penitential possibility of exile all become apparent through epic tradition.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Alex Taylor

Christopher Nolan’s new film version of The Odyssey has been a hot topic of conversation for months before its release a couple Fridays ago on July 17, and will—and should—continue to be. Some have praised the movie for its cinematic quality, while others have criticized it for its colloquial language—Odysseus’s son Telemachus and one of Penelope’s suitors Antinous both call the Ithacan king “dad” or “your daddy”—for the casting of Ellen Page (the star of Juno, who now identifies as a man and goes by “Elliot”) as an Ithacan soldier, or for changes Nolan has made to the Greek epic. But we will not have arrived at an understanding of what Nolan has done in making the film until we grasp that his re-vision of Homer’s Odyssey is deeply indebted to the later epic tradition that followed it, particularly Virgil’s Aeneid. If we see how Nolan sets out to retell the story of Odysseus’s nostos or homecoming from our side of those epics, the beauty of his telling’s portrayal of the good of hospitality, the danger of rational control’s abuse of that good, and the penitential possibility of exile all become apparent to us.

When discussing films of this kind which rely largely on a past work, whether a novel or an epic or a medieval romance, we tend to call them “adaptations,” and discuss the relative “faithfulness” of the movie to the original. It is, however, more fruitful and more true to reality to see the films, if they are true works of art, as not merely adaptations of the prior work to a new medium—the screen—but adaptations of the older story to a new vision, relating that work through the whole literary tradition to our present moment. What Nolan is doing, as Clarence Brown wrote of a different author, is “advanc[ing] the frontier of vision by creating something new out of the resources of a strong tradition.” Looking only for the old will produce disappointment. For instance, friends of mine weren’t pleased that David Lowery’s film The Green Knight (2021) did not replicate the joyous tone of the original medieval poem, but, as I argued at the time, this shift in atmosphere to the world of the old-English poem Beowulf was done by design, to show twenty-first century Americans something about ourselves through the art of film. 

Likewise with Nolan’s Odyssey—it does not take place in the elegant, polychromatic Greek world of the poleis, the city-states, filled with gods, but in the darker, more ambiguous world of Rome imagined by Virgil in his Aeneid. While Homer’s epic reveals to its audience and its characters the actions of gods—from Poseidon’s displeasure at Odysseus to Athena’s intercession to Hermes’s embassy to Calypso to set the “man of many turns” free to pursue the last stages of his homeward voyage—Virgil generally conceals divine action from his characters, even as he occasionally pulls back the curtain to his readers. Aeneas is famously frustrated when his mother, Venus, after disguising herself as a Tyrian huntress and telling him about the ways of Carthage and Dido its queen, lets her mask slip briefly before slipping away. “Why do you cheat your son so many times, / Cruel one, with visions false? Why may we not / Join hand to hand, speak and hear truthful words?” Aeneas cries out to her.

Nolan’s Odysseus and audience seldom or never see the gods. The only divine presence to manifest herself is Athena, but not in the guise of Mentor appearing to Telemachus, as Homer would have it, but occasionally to Odysseus, more full of disappointment than counsel, and a scene towards the movie’s end suggests that what the king of Ithaca sees is more a projection of Athenaic presence than the face of the goddess herself. The cinematic epic takes place in a world like that of the Aeneid, the apparently disenchanted world of the American empire, where clever technological ruses have introduced something hostile to civilization within its walls, whether we think of the impact of smartphones and social media on our young people’s mental health, the affect no-fault divorce laws have had on our nation’s family formation and the fertility crisis which has arisen, or how influencer culture and AI chatbots have created a “second cave” of opinion which masquerades as knowledge and sophistication. 

Its citizens, like ourselves, have too often closed themselves off from God by living in pursuit of ends without regard to the injustice of the means. Nolan’s Odysseus mentions to Penelope in an early scene that Agamemnon’s interest in war with Troy is not simply the injustice apparently done his brother Menelaus by the Trojan prince Paris’s absconding with Menelaus’s wife Helen, but rather an interest in gaining an economic hegemony currently possessed by Troy over maritime trade. After almost ten years of war, Odysseus, whom Homer’s Zeus says “is beyond all other men in mind,” comes up with a trick to win the war, the Trojan Horse. “One man’s idea,” Nolan’s Odysseus will say, that brings civilization crashing down.

Nolan’s genius consists in his realizing something fundamental about the Trojan Horse that isn’t even implicit in either Homer or Virgil. One of the fundamental virtues of Western Civilization, from the Greeks to the Romans to Jews and Christians, is hospitality, or xenia. In the Iliad, we see Greek and Trojan soldiers, who, upon realizing that they and their families are guest-friends—having enjoyed each others’ hospitality at table, by the hearth, and in provision of a place to sleep—forebear to fight each other, and this after nine years of brutal warfare. The author of the letter to the Hebrews (certainly with Abraham’s hospitality in mind) advises his audience, “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by doing that some have entertained angels without knowing it.” Hospitality includes the giving of gifts to mark the occasion. As Nolan’s Sinon says—to the best of his knowledge—the horse has been left as a gift to Athena, but as Odysseus later realizes, his genius tactic perverted the nature of the gift; he hid within what should be a pure offering the corruption of “ten years of rage,” waiting to pour out and destroy the city. “We violated all that’s ever sacred between people,” he tells Penelope. To welcome the stranger as if he might be a god—as if he might be made in the image of God—is to accept a gift without guile, but the “trick” of the horse has undermined that civilizing trust, sapping Western Civilization of its meaning.

Odysseus’s journey home is riddled by failures of hospitality, where the bonds that should tie peoples together—namely the law of Zeus (hospitality) and the concomitant civilizational goods of “palaces, trade, and language”—fail to tie but rather ensnare. As Calypso later tells Odysseus, he is a man who wants to “control his fate,” and reason is the tool he attempts to use for that purpose, but his reasoning is out of place in the world which he has helped bring into being. Nolan’s cyclops, unlike Homer’s, does not speak except after losing its eye. It gurgles in what sounds like words murmured through water the name “Poseidon.” “That thing talks? Why didn’t it talk to us before?” one of Odysseus’s men asks. “Do you talk to ants?” he replies. After escaping its cave, Odysseus and his remaining men land on an island populated by armored giants (likely referencing Homer’s Laestrygonians) which, likewise, do not speak, before arriving at Circe’s island. Circe, while explicitly invoking the hospitality of Zeus, uses her language not to communicate but to trap Odysseus’s men because she fears their nature as soldiers and what savageries they might inflict on her, Eurylochus’s attempts at kindness notwithstanding.

Once trust goes, only force remains—unless faith and intellect beyond mere instrumental reasoning can take the helm. After he’s returned to his native shape, Eurylochus tells Odysseus they shouldn’t leave Circe alive because she’s a witch. “Who gave her those powers?” the man of many ways asks. “Your gods.” One of the major actions within the soul of Odysseus throughout the movie is his relation to the gods, but as is more appropriate to a post-Christian era, the struggle has less to do with his deeds and more to do with his belief and the way faith or lack of it characterizes his acts. When one of his sailors characterizes the cyclops as a “son of Poseidon,” interpreting its difficult to understand murmurings as a prayer, Odysseus retorts, “We can’t live by omens and sacrifices.” It seems then that at the beginning of his journey, Odysseus is a secular, Western man, although Eurylochus’s response—questioning how many times he’s heard Odysseus praying to Athena during their voyage—complicates that picture. Odysseus is a man like Isaac, wrestling with belief in a purposeful cosmos which could be governed by anything rather than a place of “fires of anarchy and pain” made by his own idea.

To return home, Calypso tells Odysseus that he must take “a leap of faith,” making a raft of the remains of his ship and casting himself on the waves, accepting punishment from Poseidon, and he does. But the greater act of faith begins when Odysseus goes to the temple of Athena at Pylos to rescue Telemachus in a scene of Nolan’s invention—by doing so, Odysseus is reenacting in reverse the brutality of the taking of Troy, which includes the desecration of Athena’s temple, but here, he has come to save innocence rather than take it. Nolan’s telling of the end of the tale ties together strands from the tradition in a way that illuminates something which had been dark. In Homer’s Odyssey, our hero receives a prophecy from Teiresias in Hades that after reaching home, he will have to make a final journey to the west, traveling until he cannot see water. But the purpose of this journey is unclear. Odysseus discusses it with Penelope at the end of the epic, but they do not have an answer to that question. In the Inferno, Dante, working with Virgil’s villainous idea of Ulysses (the Roman name and imagined form of Odysseus), has the hero tell the story of his audacious quest for knowledge, being unsatisfied with the love of his wife and son, but it is hard to square this explanation with the character we know from Homer. Nolan, on the other hand, sees the purpose of this journey.

One of the distinguishing marks that separates mankind from beasts, one of the beauties of civilized life, is that we bury and honor our dead. One of the horrors of living in a world after Troy—for “to burn the walls of Troy was to burn the world,” as Odysseus says—is to live in a world where to save the living means forbearing the honor due the dead. Odysseus has to leave men’s bodies behind, in the cyclops’ cave, in Athena’s temple at Pylos, and his life is indebted to those men and the honor due them. The purpose told Odysseus for his journey west by Sinon in Hades is to make sacrifice for those he had to leave unburied. But first, Odysseus must accept a world beyond his control, where his receptive intellect works within a certain divine providence to restore the order of his city not only through his own strategy but through the sacrifices he must make to honor the dead.

In Homer’s epic, Odysseus tells the tale of his many journeys to the Phaiakians, a seafaring people who take him in after he has been set free from Calypso’s island. Nolan omits this civilization in order to show that the Odysseus whose intelligence has been at the service of destroying civilization must be turned to revitalizing it. Louise Cowan wrote that in “retelling his story imaginatively [Odysseus] interprets it for himself. He gives it the form and hence the meaning which until now it has lacked. In all his wanderings, incapable of self-criticism, he has merely repeated his mistakes. For people do not learn from experience; they learn from reflection and interpretation.” By having him share this moment with Penelope instead, Nolan shows that the learning that is needed to bring civilization back is rooted in the conversation made possible in the sacred space of marriage between man and wife, the most dangerous and important place of hospitality. Only within that place does Odysseus leave to honor his men, taking Penelope with him “in his fastest ship, with his brightest crew, to sail towards the horizon, chasing the setting sun,” in piety seeking to give thanks for his difficult homecoming.
